LF2 Online by Xôi · the fifth computer-player level

INSANE!

A computer player above CRAZY! that follows no hand-written script for any fighter. Right before the match it learns the fighter's moves from the mod's own data, then fights by predicting which blow lands, and when the opponent can guard or strike back. It works with every mod this site plays.

Play now Read the AI source Repository on GitHub

What INSANE! is

The original Little Fighter 2 has four computer levels: Easy, Normal, Difficult and CRAZY!. Its computer player is a set of rules written for the original fighters, keyed by their ids. Put it in a mod (One Piece GrandWorld, Naruto: The Setting Dawn, KT-LF2, Sx2…) and it has no idea what the new moves are, so it mostly punches, kicks and throws the odd D+A at random.

INSANE! is a fifth level, selected right after CRAZY! on the character selection screen (and in Tournament and Battle mode). It contains no line about Luffy or Naruto: everything it knows about a fighter comes from playing each of that fighter's moves itself, in a private copy of the match, before the match begins. That is why it can use the moves of mods nobody has ever written an AI for.

How to select it: on the character selection screen, cycle the difficulty Easy → Normal → Difficult → CRAZY! → INSANE!. In a network room the host picks the level; every machine in the room computes exactly the same thing, so the match and its recording (replay) always stay in sync.

How it learns and fights

All of it lives in one Lua file. There is no training step and no GPU: all of its "knowledge" is recomputed from the mod's data when a match starts, in exactly the same way on every machine.

  1. Learning the moves. For each fighter, the AI builds a small private copy of the match (just the fighter and a dummy) and presses every key combination: D+A and D+J in each direction, D+J+A, the punches, the running, jumping and dashing attacks, and the keys pressed during a move (chains, including counters out of the guard). It records where and when each move hits, how hard, what it costs in MP, when the fighter is free again, and where the things the move spawns (projectiles, clones, fields) fly.
  2. Predicting. Every frame of the match it works out which enemy attack is about to reach it (including projectiles in flight), how long the opponent stays stunned or down, whether the opponent is blinking (invulnerable), and after how many frames each of its own moves would land if started now.
  3. Choosing a move. Each move is scored: damage, the chance of being guarded, the risk that the opponent hits back before the move lands, MP cost, how long the fighter is left open afterwards. Slow moves (Luffy's 585-damage special takes 44 frames to come out) are used only when the opponent is locked down long enough. A move not yet used in the match gets a small bonus, so spectators see the whole kit.
  4. Defence and positioning. Guard or sidestep what is coming, never guard a blow that would break the guard, stand just outside the opponent's arms so it has to walk into the AI's own blow, avoid the danger zones of its quick strong moves, walk around obstacles, run when far away, jump in or dash in when an air move would land.
  5. Stances and charging. Held moves (Blackbeard's dark field, the chakra charge in Naruto) are kept as long as they serve and left in time; MP is charged when the opponent is far away or lying down.
  6. Knocked down. When sent flying, the AI flips back up early only if the landing spot is safe; if the opponent is waiting there, it lets the fall finish (a lying fighter cannot be hit), gets up during the invulnerability blink, and uses that blink to strike first.
  7. Knowing the opponent. The opponent's data says what it can do; how it plays says what it will do. During the match the AI counts what its opponent does: the blows it guards against the blows that land, how often it attacks when someone is within its reach, whether it flips up out of every fall, how much it jumps. A guard-happy opponent makes guard-breaking moves and grabs worth more and ordinary blows worth less; a passive one is walked up to instead of baited; one that always flips up is met where its roll ends. Everything is counted from the match state alone, so network games stay in sync.
  8. Weapons, teleports and a partner. A knife, stick, stone or drink lying nearby is walked onto and picked up when nothing presses; the AI plays its moves again with the weapon in hand, so it knows what the fighter does with it (swing, throw, drink) and uses it like any other move — a knife is thrown at the opponent, a drink is kept for when HP or MP run low. Moves that teleport to the enemy are aimed from where the fighter lands, not from where it stands. Two against one, the second fighter goes round to the other side so the enemy cannot guard both.
  9. Forms of a mod's own making. Many mods build a stronger form on an invisible item: Luffy's Gear Second in One Piece GrandWorld is a defend move that lays down an item nobody sees and picks it up at once, and with that item in hand every key does something else — faster runs, harder blows, a drain on MP every frame. The AI finds such moves because the item ends up in its fighter's hand, plays the form's keys in the copy too (its attacks, jumps, runs and what they chain into), measures what it burns and how fast it runs, and weighs it against the fighter's ordinary kit. A form worth it is entered when the opponent is held or far enough away, fought in with its own moves and runs, and, when its MP is about to run out, let end away from the enemy's arms. Sanji's Diable Jambe and a Rasengan formed in the hand work the same way; a form reached from inside another form (Zoro's Asura) is not learned yet.
  10. Respecting the get-up. A fallen opponent cannot be hit until it is up again, and after it rises it is invulnerable for a moment while it can already strike. Until the AI's quickest blow could land as that moment ends, it waits outside the opponent's arms instead of beside it — farther away, and longer, when its own HP is low.

Fighters whose mod ships a substantial AI script of its own (Dragon Ball Super, for one) keep that script at CRAZY! strength, because the mod's author knows their fighter better.

What INSANE! is aware of — and where it stands

A summary of what the computer player perceives, what it can do with it, and what is still to come. Each line names the version that brought it; the page's version badge above is read from the game build itself.

Awareness / abilityStatusSinceWhat it means in a fight
Its own moves, learned from the dataDonev14Every D-combo, punch, air, run and dash attack of any fighter in any mod: where and when it hits, what it costs, when the fighter is free again.
Chains, stances, charging, guard countersDonev15–16Keys pressed during a move, held moves left in time, MP charged when safe, striking out of the guard.
Jumping in and dashing inDonev16The air kit is used when a jump would land a move; the flight is computed from the fighter's own jump data.
The opponent's moves and projectilesDonev14What is about to hit, from which frame of which move, and everything in flight; its reach and danger zones shape the spacing.
Timing: stuns, knockdowns, invulnerabilityDonev15–16Attacks land as the opponent becomes hittable; flips up or stays down by the blows on their way; strikes first while blinking.
The opponent's habitsDonev19Guard rate, how pressing it is, whether it flips up: guard breakers against turtles, walking up to passive players, meeting flippers where the roll ends.
WeaponsDonev20Picks up knives, sticks, stones and drinks when nothing presses; swings, throws or drinks by what it learned with the weapon in hand.
Teleport movesDonev20Moves that teleport to the enemy (state 400) are aimed from where they land, 120 in front of the target.
Forms of a mod's own making (Gear Second, Diable Jambe)Donev21A move that leaves an item in the hand is a form: its keys, runs, MP burn and worth are learned; entered when worth it and safe, fought in, and let end out of reach. Forms inside forms (Zoro's Asura) not yet.
Get-up invulnerability spacingDonev21Stays outside a fallen or just-risen opponent's arms until its quickest blow can land again; farther and longer at low HP.
Team play (2 on 2, Stage)Partialv19–20Prefers the busy, the weak and the enemy holding a teammate; the second attacker goes round to the other side. No shared plan yet.
Healing, buff and summon moves without damagePlanned—Moves whose effect is not a hit have no score yet, so they are only used when they also charge MP or heal (drinks).
Memory across matchesNot planned—Habits are learned within a match only: a memory kept across matches would break the lock-step of network games when someone joins late.

How smart is it now? Against the mods' own computer players at CRAZY! it wins most fights (table below); against the original fighters, which CRAZY! already knows by heart, it is only somewhat ahead; a human who keeps changing habits is still the hardest opponent, because every habit it learns takes some seconds of play to show.

Benchmark results

INSANE! against CRAZY! (the mod's own computer player), 40 one-on-one games per mod over 10 different fighter pairs, 9000 frames per game at most, with a fixed random seed so anyone can reproduce the exact result.

Version 21 figures with --seed 12345 (version 20 gave 35–5, 35–5, 28–12 and 30–10, version 16 34–4, 35–4, 24–16 and 27–13 on the same games; the LuaJIT desktop build and the Lua 5.2 web build give the same result frame for frame). Luffy against Ace, lost 0–4 in version 20, is 2–2 with Gear Second. "HP left" is the average over all 40 games, lost games counting as 0. In KT-LF2 the original computer player already knows the original fighters' moves, so the two are close; in mods with new fighters it barely knows how to use them.

Source code and building on it

The whole project is MIT-licensed (the original game and the mods are not covered). The AI is a single Lua 5.2 file that runs identically on the web, Windows, Linux, macOS and Android. Read it, change it, send a pull request.

scripts/base/game/smart_ai.luaAll of INSANE!: learning (analyze, play), prediction (earliest_threat, move_hits), scoring and choosing (best_attack, attack_score, approach_attack), defence (answer), and the per-frame control loop (smart.control). scripts/base/game/ai_scripts.luaRuns a mod's own AI scripts (ai/*.as) and decides which fighters keep the mod's script instead of INSANE!. scripts/base/game/ai.luaThe original LF2 computer player (Easy to CRAZY!), for comparison. scripts/base/game/match.luaWhere the AI is called each frame (read_input) and where the fighters are learned when a match is created. scripts/base/ui/character_select.luaAdds INSANE! to the difficulty cycle (Tournament and Battle mode have their own files in the same folder). tools/ai-bench/The test bench: runs INSANE! against the original computer player in bulk, lists what the AI learned about a fighter and how often it uses each move, compares two versions of the AI file.

Good places to start

  • smart.levels: the reaction time of each level; a new level is one more line.
  • attack_score: the formula that scores a blow. To make the AI bolder or more careful, change it here.
  • danger_at, preferred_range: how the AI chooses where to stand.
  • approach_attack: jumping in and dashing in; stance_exit: held stances.
  • watch, guard_rate, pressure, flips_up: the opponent model, counted once a frame; add a habit there and use it in attack_score or the positioning.
  • weapon_to_take, over_weapon, armed_analysis, view_of: which weapon is worth picking up, and the fighter's moves re-learned with each kind of weapon in hand.
  • mode_entries, mode_drain, enter_mode, mode.worth: a form of the fighter's own making (an item of its own in hand), what its keys do, what it burns, and whether it is worth entering; the "enter mode" and "mode run" blocks of smart.control enter it and move in it.
  • Not done yet: a form reached from inside another form (Zoro's Asura) and forms that are a stance rather than an item; healing, buff and summon moves that deal no damage have no score yet (they are used only when they also charge MP or heal); 2-on-2 play is limited to choosing the enemy and the side to attack from — there is no shared plan between partners; habits are learned within a match only.
# Run the bench on your machine (see tools/ai-bench/README.md): 40 games of INSANE! against CRAZY! in the One Piece mod
openlf2 --pack onepiece.zip --mod tools/ai-bench --seed 12345 --input-trace ""

Every decision depends only on the state of the match — the AI draws no random numbers of its own — so recordings and network games always replay exactly. After changing the AI, run replaytest in the bench to make sure that still holds.

About this build

LF2 Online is the OpenLF2 build maintained by Xôi: the web page, the relay server for network rooms with its library of mods, the Vietnamese player guide, and the INSANE! computer player. INSANE! was Xôi's problem statement; Xôi tested it mod by mod and gave feedback over many versions, and the programming was done together with Claude (Anthropic). OpenLF2 itself is the open-source project of the OpenLF2 community.
